title: Your Instinct Isn’t Enough: Why Great Leaders Validate Their Gut
author: Joel Salinas
summary: Joel Salinas argues that leaders, especially in nonprofits, churches and small organisations, too often decide on instinct under pressure and that untested intuition can drift into bias. He defines gut as experience-informed judgment and data as both quantitative and qualitative measures, then makes the case that the best decisions come from where the two overlap rather than from either alone. Using an HBR article by Marcy Farrell, he notes that intuition is most reliable when the issue is ambiguous and further data will not change the decision. He lists the habits of leaders who cross-check their gut with questions about the source of the feeling and what is missing from view. The piece closes with starter metrics in team health, engagement, finance and mission impact, with a side track for writers and creators, so the reader can validate instinct without drowning in dashboards.
points: Leaders in nonprofits, churches and small organisations often decide fast on instinct, and without metrics even seasoned intuition can drift into bias.
Salinas defines gut as experience-informed judgment and data as quantitative and qualitative indicators, and argues leaders should use both rather than choose.
Drawing on an HBR piece, he says intuition should guide when data is exhausted, not when data is ignored.
His self-check questions ask what the leader is feeling and where it comes from, what data supports it, and what is missing from view.
He offers starter metrics in team health, engagement, finance and mission impact, including pulse scores, workload bandwidth, stay-factor surveys and a psychological safety index.
quotes: In leadership, especially in nonprofits, small organizations, church leadership, and even in the work of writers, many decisions are made quickly, under pressure, with limited input…. on instinct. Sometimes, that works. But without metrics, even seasoned intuition can drift into bias. And while we talk about discernment, what we often lack is definition.
Gut / Instinct: In this context, we’re talking about subconscious, experience-informed judgment. It’s not guesswork, it’s a combination of experience, education, and accumulated wisdom.

Not because we’re undisciplined, but because we’re focused on the work, on the programmatic deliverables, on rolling up our sleeves and getting our hands dirty. You feel it when: Your team makes a major shift based on a few passionate voices A new program is extended because we think “people like it” One person’s negative review causes impromptu changes because it’s urgent, and loud And part of the reason is systemic: most churches and nonprofits aren’t resourced to track KPIs. Time, energy, and relational capital go to keeping the work moving, but we fail to validate the work's impact.
But this comes at a cost. Because when we don’t verify our instincts, we start solving for symptoms, not systems.

I’ve watched it happen again and again: A creator abandons a growing series because a few readers unsubscribed, without realizing their open rates were rising. A pastor doubles down on a ministry model because “it’s what we’ve always done”, even though growth is negative, research is null, and impact unclear. A nonprofit pivots strategy based on one or two donor emails, without asking whether that story is reflective or exceptional

That’s the key: intuition should guide when data is exhausted, not when data is ignored. There is a risk of going too far on the side of metrics, to have so many dashboards and KPIs that they are ignored, or wrong KPIs lead a team into focusing on the wrong deliverables and going off course.
Great leaders don’t trust their gut blindly. They cross-check it. They ask: What am I feeling—and where is it coming from? Ask yourself: Experience? Urgency? Past success? Stress?
